title: Tables rondes : enseignements tirés en matière de santé mondiale : Rapport du Secrétariat

sections.title: Page 1

summary.text: The first page of a WHO Secretariat report to the Fifty-second World Health Assembly (document A52/DIV/10, 24 May 1999) on lessons from four public ministerial round tables held during the Assembly. The round tables covered priority-setting in the health sector, hospital investment, finding money for health, and strategies for a sustained response to HIV/AIDS.

sections.title: Page 2

summary.text: Summarizes the round table on priority-setting at the 1999 World Health Assembly, which found that setting health priorities is a complex and largely political process in which ministers face competing demands. Health ministers are not the only actors, since debt, donor conditions and finance ministries constrain spending, and stated priorities need real expenditure plans that are hard to keep in decentralized systems. Emergencies, conflict, HIV/AIDS, short-term needs such as failing hospitals, the East Asian financial crisis and steep budget falls in the former Soviet Union further complicate priority-setting.

sections.title: Page 3

summary.text: Continues the 1999 round table on priority-setting, stressing local decision-making, clear leadership, genuine consultation and the strong influence of donors, whose own agendas and earmarked funding can work against national priorities, and suggesting longer-term partnerships and aid within an overall public spending plan. It then opens the round table on hospital investment, stating that governments must ensure universal, equitable and affordable hospital care, with explicit hospital policy and a balanced network suited to each country's needs.

sections.title: Page 4

summary.text: Continues the 1999 round table on hospital investment, which called for ministries to coordinate national policy with private and not-for-profit providers, and weighed contracting out hospital services, noting possible savings but concerns about equity for the poor. It stresses management training and community involvement for hospital administrators, and identifies obstacles such as loss of qualified staff and the cost of maintaining equipment and technology. It also notes innovative financing mechanisms not yet fully evaluated, an urgent need for hospital research, and calls for WHO and countries to share experience.

sections.title: Page 5

summary.text: Opens the 1999 round table on finding money for health, noting that richer countries spend more on health and more of it publicly, that fragmented systems often give the poorest the worst care, and that health ministers must compete for budgets and win support for health as an investment. It covers external aid and new donor partnerships, prepayment schemes, and the contested question of user charges, which raise revenue and steer demand but conflict with access for those most in need.

sections.title: Page 6

summary.text: Lists ideas from the 1999 round table on managing health funds better, such as more autonomous hospitals, performance contracts, a regulatory rather than provider role for ministries, demand-side subsidies, regional cooperation, public–private partnerships, generic medicines and investment in prevention and primary care. It then opens the HIV/AIDS round table with the example of a southern African country with 22% adult HIV prevalence, and names high-level commitment, community action, a multisectoral approach, public education, 100% condom use and life-skills teaching as key to a sustained response.

sections.title: Page 7

summary.text: Continues the 1999 HIV/AIDS round table, calling for openness instead of denial, frank sex education in schools and involvement of people living with HIV, and rejecting unequal access to proven treatment. It cites the new International Therapeutic Solidarity Fund, urges joint regional price negotiations for antiretrovirals, investment in vaccines and microbicides and review of how global HIV funds are spent, and asks WHO to support prevention of mother-to-child transmission, including safe alternatives to breastfeeding.

sections.title: Page 8

summary.text: Concludes the 1999 HIV/AIDS round table with a discussion of partner notification, which participants said should not happen without the explicit consent of the person with HIV. It describes shared confidentiality with a close friend or relative as helpful, and says conflicts between privacy and the protection of others are best resolved through good counselling and action against discrimination.
